issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

Clinical Vignette: Robert

Robert was sixty-three when the world stopped making sense. He had been delivering packages across the city for nearly two decades—a steady job, a routine that suited him, a way to stay active and engaged. He knew the neighborhoods, the regulars who waved from their porches, the shortcuts through alleyways that saved him time. On a Tuesday afternoon in October, he'd stopped at a corner market to grab coffee before his final run. When he came back to his truck, a man was waiting. What happened in the next five minutes—the knife, the sudden violence, Robert on his knees bleeding from his shoulder—fractured something fundamental in how he understood the world. He had always believed that if you worked hard, stayed decent, and kept your wits about you, the world would mostly leave you alone. That belief died on that sidewalk.

In the months that followed, Robert returned to work, but not to any sense of safety. He began to doubt whether he could trust his own judgment anymore. The assault had shown him that his instincts were worthless—he hadn't seen it coming, hadn't read the situation, hadn't protected himself. What if he made the wrong call again? What if his inability to predict danger meant he would fail his wife, or himself? This gnawing self-doubt crept into decisions that had nothing to do with the assault. Should he take that route or that one? Was the customer at the door trustworthy? Could he really handle another day without something going wrong? The uncertainty became exhausting, and Robert found himself gripped by the conviction that he could not trust himself to do the right thing—that he was fundamentally unreliable now. This deep mistrust of his own judgment became the soil from which his coping strategies grew. Unable to tolerate the anxiety that came with feeling incompetent and uncertain, Robert threw himself into work with an intensity that bordered on obsession. He would leave at dawn and return after dark, filling every hour with deliveries, with the physical act of moving packages from truck to door. The busyness kept his mind occupied, gave him a sense of purpose and control when everything else felt chaotic. At night, when the work was done and there was nothing left to do, he would eat—not from hunger, but from a desperate need to fill the silence with something, anything. His wife would find him in the kitchen at midnight, standing before the open refrigerator, eating leftover pasta straight from the container, or methodically working through a box of crackers. It wasn't about appetite. It was about drowning out the thoughts that threatened to surface whenever his hands stopped moving. The weight accumulated slowly—he gained forty pounds over eighteen months—but Robert barely noticed. The eating served a purpose: it was a way to manage the distress that threatened to overwhelm him, a physical action that felt like taking control when control had abandoned him everywhere else.

The irony was that the harder he worked, the more he ate to manage the anxiety, the more isolated he became. His wife, Maria, began to worry. His knees ached from the constant movement, his blood pressure climbed, and the distance between them widened. He would come home exhausted, eat dinner alone in the kitchen, and fall asleep in the chair. The job that had once defined him as reliable and steady had become a fortress—a place where he could hide from the terrifying uncertainty of his own mind. By the time Robert finally agreed to see someone, he was seventy-seven and worn down in a way that no amount of work could fix. He came in because Maria had insisted, because she was frightened by the weight he'd gained, the isolation, the sense that her husband was disappearing into a fog of hypervigilance and compulsive activity. What he feared most was not the memory of the assault itself—he had become skilled at pushing that away—but the possibility that he would never again trust himself to navigate the world safely, that he had become the kind of person who could not be relied upon, even by himself.
